summary: Specifies the ForCES protocol, used between Control Elements and Forwarding Elements inside a network device, which splits the brains of a router from the packet-moving parts. It also states requirements for the Transport Mapping Layer. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: A router is split into a boss who decides and workers who carry things, and this is the language they use to talk.

questions: control element and forwarding element protocol
what is a control element and forwarding element
what is a logical function block
how does the forces heartbeat work
subtitle: The language a network device's control brain uses to program and monitor the parts that actually forward packets.

tldr.problem: Inside a network device, the control functions and the packet-forwarding hardware may come from different vendors and need a standard way to exchange configuration, status and events.
tldr.mechanism: The ForCES protocol works in a master-slave mode: Control Elements (masters) configure and query Logical Function Blocks on Forwarding Elements (slaves) with TLV-encoded messages carried over a separate Transport Mapping Layer.
tldr.outcome: It gives a common message set for association, configuration, queries, events, packet redirect and heartbeats, plus transactions and high-availability rules. RFC 5810 has been updated by RFC 7121 and RFC 7391.

today: RFC 5810 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 7121 and RFC 7391. It has not been obsoleted, and it relies on separate TML documents such as RFC 5811 and the FE model in RFC 5812.

sections.title: Separating Control from Forwarding
sections.content:
Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) defines an architectural framework and protocols to standardize information exchange between the control plane and the forwarding plane in a ForCES Network Element (NE). The requirements are in RFC 3654 and the framework is in RFC 3746. In this RFC, "the ForCES protocol" means only the protocol between Control Elements (CEs) and Forwarding Elements (FEs).

The protocol works in a master-slave mode: FEs are slaves and CEs are masters. A CE is a logical entity that uses the protocol to instruct one or more FEs how to process packets, and handles functions such as running control and signaling protocols. An FE uses the underlying hardware to do per-packet processing as directed by the CE.

What a CE controls inside an FE is described by the FE model of RFC 5812, which defines Logical Function Blocks (LFBs) in XML. The protocol carries LFB configuration components, capabilities and events. It does not apply to CE-to-CE, FE-to-FE or manager communication.
sections.eli5: One part of the machine thinks and decides, another part moves things along. ForCES lets them be built separately and still understand each other.

sections.title: Layers, Elements and Transport Requirements
sections.content:
The ForCES interface has two pieces. The Protocol Layer (PL) is the protocol proper: its messages and semantics are defined in this RFC. The Transport Mapping Layer (TML) carries PL messages and handles reliability, congestion control, multicast and ordering. The TML itself is not defined here, but the RFC lists what any TML must provide. Implementations MUST implement the SCTP-based TML of RFC 5811.

The TML requirements cover reliability (configuration traffic needs strict reliability, while redirected packets or heartbeats may tolerate loss), security, congestion control, addressing, high-availability support, encapsulation, prioritization and node overload prevention. The TML MUST authenticate CEs and FEs, and SHOULD provide message authentication and confidentiality, using TLS or IPsec. It is expected to handle up to 8 priority levels and MUST NOT re-order config packets of the same priority.

Outside the protocol sit the CE Manager and FE Manager. They supply parameters before the protocol starts, in a pre-association phase that can be as simple as reading a static configuration file. The CE and FE then enter the post-association phase and talk using the protocol.
sections.eli5: There is the message itself, and there is the van that delivers it. This RFC describes the messages and lists what the van has to promise, like not losing the important ones.

sections.title: The Common Header
sections.content:
Every protocol message starts with a common header, followed by one or more TLVs. All fields are in network byte order, and integers are unsigned.

The header holds a 4-bit version (currently 1), 4 reserved bits that senders set to zero, an 8-bit Message Type, a 16-bit Length counted in 4-byte units, 32-bit Source ID and Destination ID, a 64-bit Correlator and 32 bits of Flags.

IDs are unique across the NE. The top two bits split the space: 0x00000000 to 0x3FFFFFFF for FEs, 0x40000000 to 0x7FFFFFFF for CEs, and the top range for multicast and broadcast IDs. 0xFFFFFFFD addresses all CEs, 0xFFFFFFFE all FEs and 0xFFFFFFFF everything in the NE.

The correlator is a cookie set by the CE. The FE copies it into the matching response, so the CE can pair requests with answers. The flags include a 2-bit ACK indicator (NoACK, SuccessACK, FailureACK, AlwaysACK), a 3-bit priority from 0 to 7 (normal is 1), a 2-bit execution mode, an atomic-transaction bit and a 2-bit transaction phase.
sections.eli5: Each message has an envelope that says what kind of message it is, who sent it, who it is for, and a ticket number so the answer can be matched to the question.

sections.title: TLVs, Paths and LFB Selection
sections.content:
The body of a message is built from TLVs (type, length, value). Each TLV has a 16-bit type and a 16-bit length, and its value may itself contain TLVs. TLVs and ILVs, a variant whose type is a 32-bit local index, MUST be 32-bit aligned, with zero padding. The RFC points out that TLVs let old implementations skip new TLVs and new ones skip old ones.

To act on something in an FE, a message first picks an LFB with an LFBselect TLV holding an LFB Class ID and an LFB Instance ID. Inside it, one or more operation TLVs say what to do. Each operation names its target with a path: a series of 32-bit component IDs, written in dot notation such as 1.2.3.4. Table rows can be addressed by index or by a content key.

The operations are SET, SET-PROP, DEL, GET, GET-PROP, their -RESPONSE forms, REPORT, COMMIT, COMMIT-RESPONSE and TRCOMP. Data travels in FULLDATA-TLV (every component present, in the order the LFB defines) or SPARSEDATA-TLV (only some components, each with an ILV). Results travel in RESULT-TLV, whose value is a code such as E_SUCCESS (0x00), E_LFB_UNKNOWN (0x05), E_INVALID_PATH (0x08) or E_READ_ONLY (0x0C).

A SET with a zero-length value is not a delete. To delete, a CE must use DEL.
sections.eli5: A message says which machine part it means, what to do to it, and exactly which drawer inside it, like a street address with a house number and a room.

sections.title: The Message Types
sections.content:
The protocol defines a small set of messages, each with a fixed direction.

  • Association Setup (FE to CE) asks to join the NE and always gets a response. An FE may set its source ID to 0 to ask the CE to assign it an FE ID. Association Setup Response carries a result: 0 success, 1 FE ID invalid, 2 permission denied.
  • Association Teardown ends an association and carries a reason such as 0 (normal teardown by administrator), 1 (loss of heartbeats) or 255 (other or unspecified).
  • Config (CE to FE) sets or deletes LFB components and subscribes to events. Config Response returns per-component results.
  • Query (CE to FE) reads components or properties with GET and GET-PROP, and Query Response returns them. A query always expects a full response.
  • Event Notification (FE to CE) reports subscribed events asynchronously.
  • Packet Redirect moves data packets plus meta data between CE and FE, usually control packets or packets needing exception handling.
  • Heartbeat is a header with an empty body, used to show liveness.

Two special LFBs exist in every FE: the FE Protocol LFB (class ID 0x2, instance 0x1) controls the protocol itself, and the FE Object LFB holds facts about the FE, such as its state.
sections.eli5: The boss and workers have a handful of kinds of notes: "I want to join", "do this", "tell me that", "something happened", "here is a parcel" and "I am still here".

sections.title: Execution Modes, Transactions and Heartbeats
sections.content:
The execution mode flag tells the FE how to treat a batch of operations in one message. execute-all-or-none rolls back everything if any operation fails. execute-until-failure stops at the first failure without undoing earlier work. continue-execute-on-failure keeps going whatever happens. The RFC warns that all-or-none used carelessly can cause traffic loss.

For transactions that span several messages or several FEs, the protocol supports two-phase commit. The CE sends Config messages with the atomic-transaction flag set, marked start (SOT), middle (MOT) and end (EOT). The FE only validates them. After all FEs acknowledge, the CE sends COMMIT in the EOT message, the FE executes and answers with COMMIT-RESPONSE, and the CE finishes with TRCOMP, which the FE MUST NOT answer. A failure, or a missing reply within the timeout, makes the CE abort on all FEs. All messages in a transaction must use all-or-none mode.

For scale, the protocol allows batching several commands in one PDU and pipelining: the CE may send any number of messages before acknowledgments return, matching them by correlator.

Heartbeats are traffic sensitive: one is sent only if no other protocol traffic crossed the link within the configured interval. The CE can ask an FE for a reply with AlwaysACK, similar to ping. Defaults in the FE Protocol LFB include a CE Heartbeat Dead Interval of 30 s and an FE Heartbeat Interval of 500 ms.
sections.eli5: When the boss makes a big change, the workers first say "yes, I could do that". Only when everyone agrees does the boss say "now!", so no one is left half-changed.

sections.title: Association Phases and High Availability
sections.content:
An FE starts in the pre-association phase, then sends Association Setup. Once the CE accepts it, the CE queries capabilities and topology and can push an initial configuration. The FE reports OperEnable when it is ready to process packets. The CE can pause it by setting AdminDisable, and the FE MUST NOT process packets while in that state.

Loss of connectivity is detected by the TML or by heartbeats, and counts as loss of association. What happens next is set by the CE failover policy. With policy 0 (the default) the FE returns to pre-association at once. With policy 1, the FE moves to a not-associated state, may keep forwarding, and tries to reconnect to its primary or backup CEs until the CE Failover Timeout Interval expires (default 300 seconds). In this version of the protocol, an FE that re-associates MUST discard its old state and fetch new state, a choice made for simplicity.

Only one primary CE controls the FEs at a time, though there may be secondary CEs. The TML handles link-level failover, and the PL handles CE failover. A CE-to-CE synchronization protocol is out of scope.
sections.eli5: If the boss disappears, a worker can either stop work at once or keep going for a while and look for a backup boss. If the backup never shows up in time, the worker stops.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The framework document, RFC 3746, covers the threats in detail, and this RFC refers to it rather than repeating it. The protocol layer relies on the TML for endpoint authentication, message authentication and confidentiality, which are transparent to the PL. Security is session controlled: once a level is chosen, it applies for the whole session. Operators should use the same policies on primary and backup CEs and FEs.

The RFC defines a "No Security" level, which every CE and FE MUST implement. It consists only of error checks, not cryptography: an FE MUST connect only to CEs configured through the FEM, and receivers MUST check the CE or FE identifiers in the header. The RFC suggests this level for endpoints within a single box. Otherwise, the operator picks a TML security service, and the details depend on the TML.
sections.eli5: The messages are very powerful, so the delivery van has to check who is who and keep the messages secret. If everything is inside one box, simple name checks are enough.

fields.name: rsvd
fields.desc: Senders set to zero; receivers ignore.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Header plus the rest of the message, in 4-byte units.

fields.name: Source ID
fields.desc: NE-wide unique ID of the sender.

fields.name: Destination ID
fields.desc: NE-wide unique ID of the receiver.

fields.name: Correlator[63:32]
fields.desc: Upper half of the 64-bit cookie matching responses to requests.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: ACK, priority, execution mode, atomic transaction and transaction phase.
